en: Preface to the *Lengyan jing zhizhang shu* (Commentary on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*:
Pointing at the Palm), composed respectfully by the junior disciple Da Tian Tong Li of Xian Zong at Nianhua Temple in the Capital;
his dharma-heir disciples are Xing Zong Zu Wang Teng Qing Huai Ren and Zu Yu Jiao Zi.
Originally, when the site of enlightenment was first realized and the perfect sound was briefly proclaimed, it was like the rising sun first illuminating the high mountains;
yet, just as a great downpour does not sprout from rotten seeds, so too did the *Vaipulya* scriptures temporarily illuminate the Black Mountains, subduing their inferior minds.

Prajñā fills the great resolve. As one prepares to carry out the final testament, it is necessary to follow the wondrous and capable path. Desiring to immerse the mind in samādhi, he then expounded this teaching.
At the Jetavana Vihāra, he assembled the worthy ones who were in accord with the Dharma. Taking the precepts as the cause of concentration, he demonstrated the initiation of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.
Since lust obstructs the realm of dhyāna, he untied the bonds of craving through the *uṣṇīṣa-mantra*. Ānanda fell into a state of delusion; [the Master] verified the many...

Hearing that those who ward off evil lacked the power [to do so], he dispatched Miaode (Guṇadatta) to rescue them; thus it was revealed that through great wisdom one can advance in the Way and achieve perfection.

This constitutes the summary of the main intent of the sutra, which concludes the introductory section. As we reach the "Correct Teaching" (Zhengzong), ancient masters have offered divergent judgments. Like those who grope for an elephant and obtain only its likeness, or like those who discuss milk and fail to distinguish its true nature, their views remain incomplete.
Now, this commentary humbly follows the example of Qingliang (Chengguan), dividing the root sutra into four parts. The first is the "Revelation" (Kaishi).

The first section establishes the division of faith through *śamatha*. The second reveals the division of understanding through *samādhi*. The third reveals the division of cultivation through *dhyāna*.
The fourth reveals the division of realization through the *Śūraṅgama*. Within the first section, Ānanda returns to his own chamber of desire and piteously requests the wondrous concentration;
the Tathāgata then opens up the source of the Way and inquires about the original mind, based on what Ānanda has expressed.

Regarding the mind: because one contemplates it through the perception of signs, the mind gives rise to attachment and delight. The Tathāgata then shows warning and rebukes this as employing various false imaginings;
these perceptions are not true. Thus, in seven successive rounds, he refutes its non-existence and confronts it directly, denouncing it as not being the mind.

Having realized that by distancing himself from sensory objects he could infer their lack of substantiality, Ānanda again shed tears of sorrow. He lamented to himself: "Though I have left the household life, my mind has not entered the Way.
Thus, what he had previously grasped as his own mind and taken to be the essence of meditative concentration suddenly vanished from him.

Consequently, he sought further the nature of the mind that is quiescent and eternal, and prayed specifically for the manifestation of the wondrously luminous mind. The Tathāgata then revealed it to him.
The tranquil and eternal nature of the mind resides within the six sense-faculties; the wondrously luminous, original mind is not separate from the four natures.

Therefore, by means of the radiating light of the *svastika* symbol, he draws it forth to manifest before him. As the golden fists shine in mutual brilliance, he points them out so that [the disciple] may personally realize it.

Through ten successive profound demonstrations, he resolves many kinds of doubts. Having realized that the seeing-nature is itself the true mind, one gains self-confidence in its inherent luminosity, leaving no room for seeking it elsewhere.

It is simply because true vision is obscured by deluded vision, and wondrous clarity is shrouded by ignorance. This is like gold within ore that still requires smelting and refining, or jade in its raw state that must yet be carved and polished.
Desiring to strip away and dissolve these deluded views, I have specifically taken this sublime analogy to bring forth illumination.

To illustrate individual karma, one may cite the vision of a lamp-halo by those with red-eye disease; to illustrate commonality, one points to the perception of calamitous signs due to adverse conditions.

Once these two delusions have been eliminated, the single reality remains vividly present. Yet, doubts regarding "conjunction" and so forth still persist; therefore, these are further analyzed and refuted in succession.

That seeing-nature is the mind—this has been established through faith from this point onward. Fearing that one might cling to this nature as being restricted to the six sense faculties and fail to realize that its essence permeates all phenomena, I shall further demonstrate their convergence and integration to expand the power of your faith.
By integrating the four categories, I clarify that the fundamental reality of all dharmas is true suchness; by fusing the seven elements, I reveal that the single nature is inherently omnipresent.
This culminates in Ānanda’s recitation of verses in praise of the Buddha and his expressions of vows to repay the Buddha's kindness—all of which are true suchness.
When a phoenix first hatches, it desires at once to soar upon the clouds. How could those fledglings of swallows, wagtails, and doves possibly speak of such a thing?

Yet, while their inverted perceptions have been eliminated, their subtle delusions remain unexamined; I hope you will further scrutinize and remove them. Ānanda did not have the opportunity to inquire in detail.

Excellent is your inquiry. Pūrṇa, you have thus initiated this discourse by investigating the causes for the arising and succession of the myriad dharmas and interrogating the reason for the perfect interfusion of the five great elements.

The Tathāgata replies that the succession of arising is not distinct [from its source], that the primary factor is the clarity of awakening, and that this perfect interfusion is nothing other than itself.

This accords with the truth and is sufficient to lead one there. If one knows that the three Tathāgata-garbhas have been mutually penetrating from the very beginning, then the continuity of birth and the non-continuity of birth, as well as the perfect fusion and the lack of perfect fusion, are all merely the mind of what is known attempting to fathom unsurpassed bodhi, using worldly language to attempt to enter the knowledge and vision of true awakening.
Therefore, the Tathāgata rebuked them for not diligently seeking the unsurpassed.
The mention of Bodhi and so forth also expresses a profound sense of exhortation. When Pūrṇa doubted that there could be causes for the false, the Tathāgata taught him through sudden enlightenment;
when Ānanda clung to the real as being self-existent, the Tathāgata admonished him with gradual cultivation.

This was likely to provide a diagnosis for those who are attached to phenomena while deluded about principle, or who are hindered by principle while neglecting phenomena, and thus to prescribe the appropriate medicine. For this reason, Ānanda—

All doubts and delusions were eliminated; his mind awakened to the true reality (*dharmatā*), and his body and mind attained lightness and ease (*praśrabdhi*). He experienced what he had never before encountered.
Up to this point constitutes the section on "Opening and Showing *Śamatha* to Establish Faith," which the *Zhengmai* (Orthodox Pulse) judges as the teaching of *śamatha*.

However, although correct faith has been established, if one relies solely on the holy teachings as the definitive authority, wondrous awakening is difficult to evoke; it requires the cultivation of contemplation based on principle (*yuktipratyavekṣā*) to polish and refine it.
The assembly, likened to a magnificent hall, requested to enter its gates; the Tathāgata, out of compassion for the congregation, opened the path of cultivation.
He divided the gates to establish two meanings: namely, that by making the cause identical to the fruit, one establishes the excellent method for clarifying turbidity and entering Nirvāṇa;
and by untangling the knots from their roots, one provides the wondrous path for shedding entanglements and entering perfect penetration. He verified these points to resolve two doubts, for...

Whether in motion or stillness, waking or sleeping, the fundamental auditory nature is inherently uninterrupted; apart from seeing, feeling, hearing, and knowing, there is no separate "knot" to be untied.

The binding of the scarf was used to demonstrate the sequence of stages, for it serves to show how delusion arises from the True and how one returns to the True by reversing that delusion—how birth proceeds in a forward order and cessation follows a reverse order, each with a sequence that must not be disordered. This was a profound instruction for selecting the fundamental source.

The faculties and hindrances are the gateway of the ear-door of Avalokiteśvara; they possess the threefold reality and are fit to be used for teaching Ānanda and those sinking in the delusions of the final age.
By this means, the assembly’s body and mind have become clearly illuminated, and each has recognized the path home—the traces of Ānanda’s own mind.

Yuanming’s Sudden Enlightenment Dharma Gate for Accomplishing Buddhahood: A Prayer to Deliver Beings Sunk in the Final Age. He again requested the ritual protocols for the site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
The Tathāgata showed him four kinds of clear instructions, admonishing that these must first be strictly observed.

Therefore, he taught that taking the gathering of the mind as the precept gives rise to concentration (*samādhi*) through the precept, and wisdom (*prajñā*) is awakened through concentration. Thus, demonic activities cannot cause disturbance, and the site of practice can be successfully accomplished.
Should habitual tendencies prove difficult to eliminate, one must still construct a ritual altar, recite mantras, and perform the practices according to the Dharma.

The Buddha will surely manifest his body, bestowing both exoteric and esoteric empowerment, so that wondrous awakening arises spontaneously. Although the boundaries of the ritual site pertain to phenomenal appearances, these signs are employed to symbolize the ultimate reality.

One must especially apply oneself with meticulous care and purity to the arrangement and establishment [of this teaching], so that all may follow the Buddha’s intent and transmit it to the Dharma-ending age as an eternal model.
Ānanda, reflecting back on how he was saved, realized it was entirely due to the inconceivable power of the *dhāraṇī*; he thus requested once more that [the Buddha] expound it.
The Tathāgata again emitted light from the crown of his head.

Relying upon the unobstructed mind of the emanation Buddhas, he specifically proclaimed this teaching and further praised its vast merit and extolled its great benefits. All Buddhas are born from this; all transgressions are extinguished by means of it.
There is no difficulty that is not resolved, no Māra that is not subdued, no obstruction that is not removed, and no practice that does not reach fulfillment.
It is therefore fitting that the assembly of sages attend upon him and the hundred spirits protect him. Up to this point has been the section on "Revealing Samādhi and Attaining Liberation."
Thus, Zhengmei judges this to be the teaching on samādhi. However, once wondrous awakening has been achieved, one must exert oneself in true cultivation.

Thereupon, Ānanda requested clarification regarding the stages, which are briefly divided into four categories: first, what is meant by the forty-four minds of the stage of "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-vijñāna-bhūmi*);
second, reaching what gradual sequence does one obtain the designation of "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*); third, arriving at what location is it called...
Entering into the stages [of the bodhisattva path]. Fourth: What is meant by the term "Equal Enlightenment Bodhisattva"?

The Tathāgata expounds upon this in contrast with them, clarifying the fundamental causes of ascent and descent, and providing a detailed analysis of delusion and awakening to point out the pivotal essentials of the sage and the ordinary person.

This is because the nature is luminous and perfect; fundamentally, there is neither ordinary nor sage, nor ascent nor descent. It is only because the nature is manifested through conditions that there exist the worlds.

The realms and all sentient beings are characterized by false and delusive thoughts; these are eliminated through the three gradual stages. This answers the question of at what gradual stage one attains the vision of practice.

When the craving for desire is withered away and there is nothing but pure wisdom—passing through the stages of faith, abiding, practice, and direction, and perfecting the four levels of added effort—this answers the question of why this is called the "ground of dry wisdom. It refers to the forty-four minds, beginning from the Stage of Joy.

Reaching as far as the Far-Going (Dūraṃgamā) stage, and by means of immovability reaching the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā)—this answers the question of what it means to "proceed toward a destination" when one enters the stages (*bhūmi*).
When the limits of awakening intersect, it is called Equal Awakening (*Samyaksambodhi*)—this answers the question of why a Bodhisattva is called an "Equal-Awakened One.
However, the final secure barrier does not depart from the very first step; therefore it is said: "This awakening is the initial attainment of the Vajra."

Within the mind, this is first the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi*). It is further stated that "it is precisely through these three progressive stages that one is well able to accomplish the fifty-five positions.

Thus, we know that in the practice and realization of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, the primary emphasis lies upon the initial resolve. Upon careful examination of its purport, the first two progressive stages correspond to the aforementioned four kinds of clear instructions;
the third progressive stage corresponds to the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) of the site of enlightenment (*maṇḍala*). These preparatory practices...
There is no difference; it is simply by relying on the samādhi of the ear-gate that one unties the six knots and transcends the three emptinesses.

From the stage of Dry Wisdom (śuṣka-vijñāna) onwards, the fifty-five stages are all cultivation subsequent to enlightenment. Cultivation is non-cultivation; realization subsequent to enlightenment is non-realization.

This is merely a brief indication of the sequential arrangement within the context of perfect interfusion. Having completed the answers to the questions, the summary of the essential meaning is largely concluded.
Thus, at Mañjuśrī’s request for names, the Tathāgata summarized and indicated five types, admonishing him to uphold them.
Up to this point constitutes the section on the exposition of the cultivation of *dhyāna*; it is precisely what the *Zhengmai* (The Correct Pulse) designates as the "Exposition of *Dhyāna*.

According to the three names requested by Ānanda, the Tathāgata has explained each one in detail; how much more so since he has already provided the names and exhorted their upholding—the remainder should likewise be understood.
There is no such teaching. That it is not so now is because of the Tathāgata’s secret cause.

Having long been submerged in the seven realms of existence, even if one does not realize that these seven realms are fundamentally empty, even if one were to briefly believe it, it would not be definitive. Thus Ānanda asked his question, once again supporting *śamatha*, saying:
"If this wondrously bright, truly pure, and wondrous mind has from the beginning been all-pervading and perfect, then everything is nothing other than [this mind]."
The essence of the Buddha; the essence of the Buddha is reality. How then can there be the paths of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, and devas?
The Tathāgata has shown that internal attachment is "feeling" (*qing*) and external yearning is "perception" (*xiang*).

If perception is pure, one immediately ascends and will certainly be born in the heavens. If perception is predominant and feeling is slight, one rises lightly and flies afar, becoming a flying immortal (*fei-xian*).
The Great Power Ghost King, the flying yakṣas, and the earth-walking rākṣasas—should their emotional desires (*kāma*) and thoughts (*saṃjñā*) be equal, they will be born among humans.

Should their emotions be many and thoughts few, they will flow into the realm of animals. Should there be seven parts emotion and three parts thought, they will sink below the water-wheel and become hungry ghosts.

Should there be nine parts emotion and one part thought, they will descend through the fire-wheel; with a light degree of emotion, they are born in the *sāntara* hells, and with a heavy degree, they are born in the *avīci* hells.

If one is purely of emotional nature, one immediately sinks into the Avīci Hell. Next, it clarifies that by creating the ten causes of habitual action, one undergoes the sixfold intersecting retributions.
Those who are "purely of emotional nature" and sink, as well as those with nine thoughts and one perception, will eventually exhaust their offenses and take the forms of various ghosts.

Those with seven perceptions and three thoughts who sink beneath the water-circle encounter their karmic adversaries and become animals to repay their debts. This refers to those whose emotional nature predominates...
Few are those who, having flowed into transmigration among animals, receive full retribution and return to human form within the human realm, merging with the ten classes of beings.
Those whose emotions and thoughts are equal are born among humans. Those who preserve their thoughts to solidify their forms constitute the ten kinds of *ṛṣis*.

Those whose emotions are slight and thoughts predominant, yet who can levitate without traveling far, include those of the six heavens of desire, the four dhyānas, and the various four *ārūpya* concentrations. Those who consist purely of thought fly directly [to higher realms].

Regarding those born in the heavens up to the asuras, since these constitute four destinies (gatis), the degree of their emotional and conceptual attachments can likewise be known according to these four destinies.
However, all of these are merely the characteristics of conditioned existence; they are births received through false imagination.

Within the wondrous, perfect, and luminous, unconditioned fundamental mind, they are all like flowers in the sky—originally non-existent. One who understands this meaning [realizes] the secret cause of the Tathāgata’s permanence.

It manifests before one; through the certainty of right faith, *śamatha* is accomplished. Furthermore, because the noble nature is universally pervasive, both following and reversing [the sense organs] serve as skillful means.
Yet, Avalokiteśvara stands alone: the faculty of hearing is the most perfectly penetrating.

However, one must guard against the six knots being about to untie, when right mindfulness and deluded thoughts arise together, and the five aggregates are about to open, such that internal demons and external obstacles may coincide.

The Māras rose up in competition. Thus, as the Tathāgata was about to conclude his session upon the Dharma-seat, he turned toward the Purple Gold Mountain and, once again giving rise to his genuine compassion, returned to lean upon it.

He revealed the causes and conditions for the manifestation of Māras, supported the cultivation and realization of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), and analyzed their characteristics in detail, instructing them on how to recognize them in advance.
When those shadowy states appear before you, you must by all means avoid falsely claiming them to be holy realizations; rather, pass through each and every one of them.

Throughout the stages of perfect illumination, should one happen to attain a small measure and dwell complacently in that abundance—mistaking a thief for a son—it goes without saying that celestial demons, ghosts, spirits, heterodox sects, and external paths will suffice to harm the Dharma-body;

even such ones as the śrāvakas of fixed nature and the pratyekabuddhas will sever the seeds of Buddhahood. This is what is meant by "destroying your entire precious body of enlightenment. You must know this.
The destruction of the *skandhas* occurs within the unraveling of the fetters. As it was said previously: "At the outset, within hearing, one enters the stream and loses the object of perception.

Once that which is entered has become still, movement and stillness do not arise; this is the destruction of the *rūpa-skandha*. Continuing in this way, as the hearing and the heard are both exhausted, the *vedanā-skandha* is destroyed.

When the exhaustion of hearing does not persist and the awareness of what is aware becomes empty, the *saṃjñā-skandha* is destroyed. When the emptiness of awareness passes through to completion, the [emptiness of]..."

When that which is empty is extinguished, the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is destroyed. Once arising and ceasing have been extinguished and quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirodha*) manifests before one, the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is destroyed.

When the aggregate of consciousness is destroyed, correct understanding becomes perfect, and samādhi is accomplished. Furthermore, although the principle is realized all at once, it is eliminated simultaneously with awakening;
yet phenomena are not removed instantaneously, but are exhausted through a gradual process. If one clings to the principle and abandons phenomena, one will inevitably neglect the profound dwelling.

To dwell in the shallow while neglecting the profound results in the failure to achieve the various stages of *dhyāna*. To cling to principle while abandoning practice leaves the myriad deeds of a Bodhisattva incomplete.

This is why Ānanda earnestly requested subtle instruction, and why the Tathāgata fully revealed the limits of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), so that practitioners, after attaining perfect penetration through the faculty of hearing, may gradually cultivate through successive practices and reach their goal.
Having realized the true fruit, one must by no means claim that there is nothing more to do, lest one willingly fall into the pride of overestimation (*adhimāna*).

However, as for cultivation after awakening, it requires no strenuous effort. Just as when the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate) was exhausted previously, the various sense faculties functioned interchangeably, so too one may say that from within this mutual functioning, one is able to enter the Bodhisattva’s adamantine stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*).
The perfectly luminous and essential mind manifests its transformations therein; thus it is.
Transcending the stages of faith, abiding, practice, and penetration, one adds the grounds (bhūmis) and attains equal enlightenment, entering the Tathāgata’s ocean of wondrous adornment.

Thus, it is known that Avalokiteśvara has attained two kinds of excellence and manifested three kinds of wondrous functions; all of this is brought forth through transformation from within the perfectly luminous, essential mind.

Relying on this to traverse the stages, what difficulty or peril could there be? One who understands this meaning will not neglect the cultivation of phenomena, yet remains in meditative concentration.

That can be accomplished. Up to this point constitutes the section on the "Revelation and Realization of the Śūraṅgama. This is precisely what the *Zhengmai* (Orthodox Pulse) judges to be essential for those at the initial stage of practice.
Now that the "Correct Doctrine" (*zhengzong*) is complete, its circulation requires people; thus, seeking worthy ones for the sake of the Dharma, I specifically offer this comparative evaluation.
To compare the extraordinary merit of transforming others: the moment one gives rise to a single thought of revelation, it is equal to filling the ten directions with the seven treasures.

Even the merit of giving cannot compare to it. As for the supreme benefits of practicing it oneself, even if one were to possess both wisdom and the recitation and upholding [of the teachings], and were to exhaust the Buddha’s wondrous eloquence throughout kalpas, his virtues would still be difficult to fully extol.
Therefore, I exhort you to rely upon my words of instruction and to practice the Path according to those teachings.
One directly attains Bodhi, and no further demonic activities remain. From this point on, the profound resonance finally ceases. At that time, the assembly was filled with joy;

it should naturally circulate and spread from one to another, like a lamp whose flames divide and multiply into an infinity. (Tongli) I have enjoyed great fortune, entering the Śākya gate early in life.

I am ashamed that I lack the karmic conditions to travel through the misty waters of a hundred cities, yet I am fortunate to possess the blessing of tea and incense within a single room. May I thus savor and contemplate [this teaching].

Having received this sutra among the many scriptures, I did not measure my own talent as meager, but immediately resolved to transcribe it by hand. I sought its essential meanings in ancient commentaries and sought true standards within my own mind.
Desiring to analyze it point by point and detail by detail, I modeled my work after the method of gradual accomplishment;
furthermore, I reverently appealed to the Triple Gem, praying for their protective empowerment.
I prostrate to the Original Teacher Śākyamuni, And to the inconceivable transformation Buddhas from the light upon his crown.
The *Śūraṅgama Samādhi*, the secret essence of perfect penetration, Inspires profound principles for the multitudes of the two vehicles;
May its blessings reach the ignorant and foolish so they may accord with the holy mind. May it be analyzed in detail and explained clearly, as if pointing at one's own palm.
Circulating far and wide throughout all sentient beings, it brings benefit to self and others without end.

Now, in order to explain this sutra, ten gates will be opened: first, the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching; second, its classification within the Piṭakas and Vehicles; third, the meaning of the teaching that can encompass others;

fourth, the suitability of the faculties of those who are to be taught; fifth, the nature and depth of its essence; sixth, the general and specific characteristics of its primary intent; seventh, the [occasion of] the teaching...
Regarding the sequence: first, the eight translations, transmissions, and commentaries; second, the general explanation of the title; third, the detailed interpretation of the textual meaning.

First, concerning the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching: it means that the teaching does not arise of itself, but emerges only when there is a cause; and the cause does not sustain itself [without the teaching].

One must wait for the support of conditions; therefore, the introduction first demonstrates the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching, both in general and in detail. Regarding the general causes and conditions:
this refers to a comprehensive discussion of the holy teachings of the Tathāgata throughout his entire life, which are solely for the sake of one great matter.

As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great causal condition (ekamahā-kṛtya-hetu-pratyaya). That is to say:"

It is because he wishes to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, so that they may attain purity; because he wishes to reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to sentient beings;
because he wishes to cause sentient beings to awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; and because he wishes to cause sentient beings to enter the path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Based on this, the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world—from beginning to end—is solely for the sake of the one Buddha-knowledge and Buddha-vision; his teaching is solely the teaching thereof.
This is it. Beyond this, there is nothing further that can be said; even if anything were to be said, it would only be for this purpose.
Moreover, this applies not only to one Buddha, but to every Buddha alike; therefore, it constitutes the general causal condition.
Regarding the distinct causes and conditions: specifically concerning this sutra, there are ten purposes. First, it is to admonish those with deranged wisdom.

Now, when a practitioner loses the defensive walls of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the waves of wisdom will inevitably surge out of control. When the waves of wisdom surge out of control, they take analytical discernment as their primary function;
when the walls of concentration have collapsed, they take extensive learning as their playground. How could such a person know that merely talking about food does not satisfy hunger? Countless...

Śāriputra was constantly impoverished; in the end, he fell into perverse thoughts and found it difficult to escape the net of craving. For his sake, this sutra is preached to warn against such wild wisdom.

It is like Ānanda, who returned from the chamber of lust and requested instruction on the wondrous samādhi. He first expressed regret that, from time immemorial, he had been devoted solely to much hearing (*bahuśruta*) without fully perfecting the power of the Way.
Furthermore, after selecting the various methods of perfect penetration, he said: "Even though Ānanda possesses powerful memory, he cannot avoid falling [into error]."
"Perverted thoughts" and so forth all serve as warnings against the mind of wild wisdom. ○ Second, regarding the exhortation to cultivate true samādhi: Now, wisdom itself is not inherently evil;
it must be supported by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). How could desire then be able to entangle it? It depends solely on having a foundation for true cultivation.
If one merely admires true cultivation while failing to abandon delusive conditions, then even if one forcibly restrains the conscious mind, it will ultimately not be true samādhi. This is because...
In expounding this sutra, one should apply oneself with diligent effort. As the sutra says:

"Even if one were to extinguish all seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and internally maintain a state of profound stillness, it would still be a mere reflection of the discrimination of dharma-dusts. It further says: "Though one may currently achieve the nine successive meditative attainments..."
One cannot exhaust the outflows to become an Arhat and so forth; all such efforts must strive toward cultivating the true intent of meditative concentration.

Third, because coarse delusions have been eliminated, and since false consciousness was previously entangled and the essence of seeing lost its illumination, one clung to all phenomena as being external to the mind.

Those who are deluded regarding the One True Reality may either cling tenaciously to the existence or emptiness of causes and conditions, thereby becoming bound to and falling into provisional teachings;

or they may fix their minds in a state of naturalness, yet still gallop toward externalist calculations. Both are inverted conceptions that sufficiently obstruct true cultivation. To eliminate these, the Buddha specifically preached this sutra.
As in the sutra, he refutes false consciousness to reveal true vision, harmonizing the four categories and fusing the seven elements; at the conclusion, he further rebukes [such errors].

Because the world lacks knowledge, it takes delusion as its cause and condition, as well as [the notion of] spontaneity; all such things are merely the conceptualizations and calculations of the conscious mind.
These conceptualizations and calculations constitute the "delusions of view," which are termed "coarse" because they can obstruct right faith and are termed "perversions.
As Ānanda recited the verse on the Treasury of Emptiness in confirmation of his faith: "The Wondrous, Profound, Total-Mastery, Immovable Honored One, the King of Śūraṅgama in the World..."
"How rare! It has eliminated my inverted conceptions accumulated over billions of kalpas, allowing me to attain the Dharma-body without passing through the aeons of a *saṃghī*.

While it can be understood that these coarse inverted conceptions have been eliminated, [the subtle delusions remain]. The fourth [section] examines the removal of subtle delusions. This is because while the coarse conceptions have already fallen away, the subtle delusions have not yet been eradicated.

Although one may believe that all phenomena are but mind, one has not yet thoroughly penetrated the fundamental source of the principle of "mind-only. Thus, one certainly knows the five great elements...

"Perfect fusion. Because they have not yet truly realized the profundity of perfect fusion, every stirring of thought and movement of mind immediately deviates from the essence of the Dharma and can obstruct the concentration of the nature.

These delusions are designated as "subtle"; it was for the sake of eliminating these that the Buddha preached this sutra. Regarding Ānanda, after his inverted perceptions had dissolved, the verse says:
"O Great Hero, of Great Power and Great Compassion, I pray you will further examine and eliminate the subtle delusions, so as to enable me..."
"Attaining supreme enlightenment at an early date," and so forth—this shows that Pūrṇa posed two questions concerning both types of subtle afflictions (*anuśaya*).

The Tathāgata answered each according to its cause, which constitutes a thorough elimination [of those doubts]. When Pūrṇa’s doubt reached the point of falsely attributing causes to existence, and Ānanda clung to the notion of "reality" as being self-existent, the Tathāgata again provided detailed and exhaustive instruction.
That this was for the purpose of thoroughly eliminating subtle afflictions can be clearly understood. (Fifth)

This is to select and demonstrate the perfect contemplation (*yuan guan*). Now, the threefold treasury within the one mind is the very essence of wondrous concentration, as has already been clarified above.
However, regarding the four categories and seven elements (*sì kē qī dà*), upon which should one rely as the gate of contemplation? This shall be examined next.

Third, regarding those capable of receiving the teaching: the ocean of the doctrine is vast and profound; the clouds of Dharma pervade everywhere; the light of wisdom is boundless; and its wondrous transformations are inexhaustible.
By means of words that transcend speech, it elucidates the principle where words cease; through transformations that transcend change, it responds to the myriad shifting mechanisms of the world.

As these mechanisms differ, the teachings vary; thus the meanings are divided into many types, yet there are also those that are not so divided. To grasp but a little while losing much is a great error.

Now, as I am about to provide a classification, I shall briefly divide this into three chapters: first, classifying the teachings according to their doctrinal tenets; second, debating the meanings according to the treatises;

Fifth: Among those who were both monastics and laypeople, there were eighteen schools in total. While some followed one path and others opposed it, making it difficult to exhaustively critique all other traditions, none surpasses the school of Xianshou (Xuanzang) in its refinement of facts and completeness of principle.
Therefore, relying upon the various patriarchs of this Xianzong (Dharmalakṣaṇa) school, I shall briefly outline the Five Teachings.

The first is the Hīnayāna teaching, also called the Teaching for the Two Vehicles of Ignorant Dharma. It is so named because it differs from the Mahāyāna, because it is established according to the capacities of sentient beings, and because it follows the words of others.

It explains the numerical categories of all phenomena as being exclusively distinct, using them to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, to differentiate between the noble and the ordinary, to clarify cause and effect, and to divide between what is to be sought and what is to be shunned.
However, the number of dharmas taught therein is only seventy-five; it speaks only of the emptiness of persons, and not...
Regarding the elucidation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*): although the emptiness of phenomena is indeed taught, it is not fully clarified;

for one merely establishes the roots of defilement and purity based on the six consciousnesses and the three poisons, without exhausting the source of all phenomena. Consequently, much dispute and contention arise.

Second is the Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna, also called the Partial Teaching (*bhinnadeśanā*). It merely states that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are empty, yet it does not fully exhaust the principles of the Mahāyāna Dharma; therefore, it is called "Initial.
It merely speaks of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, asserting that some attain Buddhahood while others do not; therefore, it is called "Partial.

It discusses the characteristics of phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*) extensively, while touching upon the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) only slightly. What it calls "nature" is merely one among the categories of characteristics, and it is taught as being existent.
The *Śata-dharma-viniścaya* (Decisive Analysis of the Hundred Dharmas) is clear and distinct; thus, there is little dispute regarding it.

Third is the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-naya*), also called the True Teaching (*bhūta-naya*). This refers to the elucidation that dependent origination is without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and that all things are suchness (*tathatā*).

It holds that those of fixed nature among the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) and those of no nature (*abhavya*)—the icchantikas—all shall attain Buddhahood. As this represents the ultimate discourse of the Mahāyāna, it is so named.

In conclusion, because it accords with the principle of reality, it is called "real. It discusses the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) extensively and touches upon *dharma-lakṣaṇa* (phenomenal characteristics) sparingly;

Fourth is the Sudden Teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). It holds that when not even a single thought arises, one is immediately named a Buddha; it does not teach according to the gradual progression of stages (*bhūmi*).

As the *Siyi jing* (Saṃghadeva’s translation of the *Saṃgharakṣita-sūtra*) says: "One who attains the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena does not proceed from one stage to another. The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* says:

It does not speak of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) at all, but only elucidates true nature (*tathatā*). All that exists is merely deluded thought; the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is beyond words.
The five dharmas and the three natures are all empty; the eight consciousnesses and the two kinds of selflessness are both discarded. It reviles the teachings and exhorts...

Detachment: Destroying appearances and merging the mind. To give rise to the mind is delusion; not giving rise to it is Buddhahood. Furthermore, there is neither Buddha nor non-Buddha, neither arising nor non-arising, as in the case of Vimalakīrti’s silent abiding.

Fifth is the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). This means it universally encompasses and is fully complete as the preceding four teachings. A single stage is all stages; all stages are a single stage.
At the fulfillment of the ten levels of faith, one subsumes the five stages to achieve equal and perfect enlightenment; therefore, it is called "Perfect."
What is taught here is solely the inexhaustible Dharma-realm: its ocean of nature is perfectly interfused; its dependent origination is unimpeded;

There are both general and specific aspects.

The general refers to the Buddhist teachings of a single lifetime as a whole; although the various schools have differing views that are each distinct, they are categorized according to their underlying meanings.
Furthermore, these may be condensed into six schools. 1. The School of Attachment to Phenomena According to Their Characteristics (*Svalakṣaṇadharmābhiniveśavāda*).

This refers to those who give rise to attachments of existence and non-existence regarding all persons and phenomena; namely, the various masters of the Hīnayāna. Relying on sūtras such as the *Āgama* and the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, they composed various sectarian treatises such as the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.
Within this school, there are further six sub-sects. The first is the School of the Coexistence of Self and Phenomena (*Pudgaladharma-ubhayāstitvavāda*).
These refer to the Vātsīputrīyas, Dharmottarīyas, Bhadrayānīyas, Saṃmitīyas, Gokulikas, and Haimavatas, among others.
Because they posit a self (*ātman*), the masters of the various schools collectively reject them and label them as "non-Buddhists who have attached themselves to the Buddha's Dharma.
Second, the schools that maintain both phenomena and a self, such as the Sarvāstivādins, Sthaviras, and Bahuśrutīyas, assert that all phenomena are substantially real, yet they do not posit [a self].

My [teaching] differs from the calculations of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Furthermore, I establish correct causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) in order to refute the non-Buddhists' false causes and their doctrine of causelessness.

Regarding the school that maintains the thesis that the three dharmas have no coming or going—namely, the Mahāsāṃghika, Kaukkuṭika, Caitika, Haimavata, Aparasaila, Uttarasaila, Dharmaguptaka, and Kāśyapīya schools—they assert that only present conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas exist, while past and future dharmas... [do not].
Since both essence and function are non-existent, they are not mentioned. Fourth is the school that maintains the conventional is false while the real is true; this refers to the Saṃmitīya school.

Within the aforementioned present conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), they assert that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are real, while the elements (*dhātu*) and sense-bases (*āyatana*) are conventional.

The masters of the Sautrāntika school at the end of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (addressing the Mūla-Sautrāntikas) also hold this view. Fifth is the school that maintains the conventional is false and the ultimate is true; this is the supramundane school.
The [Sarvāstivāda] schools and so forth maintain that the conventional is provisional because it is illusory; the supramundane is the opposite of this.

Sixth, the school of those for whom all phenomena are merely names (*Ekavyāvahārika*) and so forth maintains that all selves and phenomena exist only as provisional designations and lack substantial reality.

Among these six, the first maintains only existence, the last maintains only non-existence, and the middle ones maintain both existence and non-existence; therefore, they are collectively categorized as the single "Dharma according to Characteristics" (*Lakṣaṇānusāri-dharma*).
The Tenets. II. The School of the Characteristics of Consciousness-Only (*Vijñaptimātra-lakṣaṇa-nikāya*). This is because it maintains that all phenomena are merely manifestations of consciousness.
Specifically, Asaṅga and Vasubandhu, relying on the *Vaipulya*, *Saṃdhinirmocana*, and other sutras, composed the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, and so forth.

III. The School of True Emptiness and Signlessness (*Tattva-śūnyatā-nimitta-nikāya*). This is because it maintains that all dharmas are empty and signless. Specifically, Āryadeva and Bhāviveka, relying on...

The *Sūtra of Sublime Wisdom* (*Prajñāpāramitā*) and others; and the composition of the *Treatise on the Hundred Gates* (*Śata-dvāra-śāstra*) and the *Treasure of the Precious Jewel* (*Ratnagotravibhāga*).

Fourth is the school of the Mind as the Essence of the Four Collections (*catur-nikāya-citta-tathatā-pratītyasamutpāda*), which asserts that all phenomena are solely True Suchness (*tathatā*) manifesting in accordance with conditions and possessing sands-of-the-Ganges virtues.

This refers to the masters Sthiramati and Aśvaghoṣa, who, relying on sūtras such as the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, composed the *Ratnagotravibhāga-mahāyāna-uttaratantra-śāstra* and other works. Fifth is the school of the Quiescence of True Nature (*bhūtatathatā-śānti*).
The School of Extinction (Mie-zong). This refers to the direct manifestation of the essence of nature (*dharmatā*) wherein both conceptualization and its characteristics are utterly severed.

It is based on the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and other sutras that masters such as Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna composed the *Tathatāsamādhi-śāstra* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. Sixth: The School of the Perfect Interfusion of the Dharma-realm (*Dharmadhātu-yuanrong-zong*).
This refers to the inexhaustible Dharma-realm, which is like Indra’s net, with principal and satellites arrayed in successive layers, perfectly interfused and without obstruction.
Thus, Nāgārjuna and Vasubandhu, relying on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and other scriptures, composed the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* and other treatises of inconceivable depth.

Regarding these six schools, with the exception of the first within the first school—the School of Existence (Yōu-zōng)—there is no inclination toward it, as it is not accepted by the Buddha's teachings.

The others each serve as the means for specific types of practitioners to open the gate of enlightenment and support their practice, with the goal of realizing the fruit appropriate to their own category.
If one were to clarify the essential purport of this specific sutra alone, there are both general and specific aspects within it; the general aspect refers to this sutra.
It takes as its primary principle the wondrous samādhi of the perfect fusion of the non-obstructed three-in-one, which is cultivated through the nature inherently possessed by one's own mind.
Its goal is to cause sentient beings to give rise to faith, develop understanding, and initiate practice, thereby reaching the ultimate fruit. Regarding the aforementioned general [classification]:

This corresponds precisely to the fourth [section]. The fifth and sixth may also be understood as supplementary. Specifically, regarding this particular sutra, I shall briefly outline six pairs based on the sequence of shallow and deep levels, following the model of the *Zhengmai* (The Correct Pulse).
First is the pair of "Destruction and Revelation. This means that the discriminative consciousness (*vijñāna*) obstructs true concentration (*samādhi*);
therefore, the primary tenet is the total destruction of the discriminating mind. This destruction is not merely for its own sake; the underlying intent is to cause one to abandon consciousness.
First, the pair of "using the faculty" (*indriya*) and "therefore taking the ultimate manifestation of the nature of seeing as the goal. This means that for a beginner, single-mindedness is valued;

since only the faculty can be relied upon, the teaching takes the partial indication of the nature of the faculty as its thesis. Yet, this partiality does not remain partial; the intention is to lead them from the partial into the whole.
Therefore, it takes the full revelation of the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*) as its goal. Third, the pair of "faith" (*śraddhā*) and "understanding" (*adhimukti*). This refers to correct understanding.
It is difficult to give rise to [this realization]; only faith can be relied upon. Therefore, taking the perfect faith in the *tathāgatagarbha* as the primary tenet (*zong*).

This faith is not mere faith; its intent lies in causing one to develop understanding (*jie*) through faith. Therefore, taking the selection of faculties to achieve understanding as the goal (*qu*). Fourth, regarding the pair of essence and function:
to manifest the function of transforming others, one must understand the essence of universal penetration. Therefore, taking the sudden understanding of the perfect essence as the primary tenet.

The essence is not eternally quiescent; the intention is to cause it to give rise to function from that essence. Therefore, taking the manifestation of function and its formation into practice as the goal, the five practices and the single stage correspond to one another.
This means that to aspire to participate in the ranks of the sages, one must rely upon the gate of practice;

thus, taking the cultivation of practice through successive stages as the core principle, these practices are not performed in vain. The intention is to cause one to gradually realize and enter [enlightenment]; therefore, one takes the realization of the stages through successive progression as the objective.
This constitutes the "destination. The sixfold fulfillment constitutes the "pair," meaning that since the fruit is not attained instantaneously, there must necessarily be gradual stages;

therefore, the realization of these stages in parts is established as the primary theme (*piṭaka*). The non-abiding in those partial realizations is intended to lead one from the partial toward the complete;

thus, the perfection of *bodhi* is established as the destination. This represents the progression from the former to the latter, where they arise in successive order, together forming the central theme and purpose of this single scripture.
One who understands this proceeds from the shallow to the deep; through faith, understanding, cultivation, and realization, one will not suffer the defect of leaping over stages.
This concludes the section on the general and specific aspects of the fundamental purport.
Seventh, regarding the sequence of time before and after in teaching: When the mind merges with the Ultimate Way, it is undifferentiated throughout past and present.

Through the realization of non-arising (*anutpāda*), time itself is fundamentally non-existent. Yet, relying on the Way to accomplish transformation, from non-arising there manifests apparent arising; thus, the Dharma is applied according to the capacity of the recipient.
Explanations are established based on temporal divisions. According to the scriptural system, there are two types of temporal divisions:

the specific and the general. Within the specific, there are three [divisions]. First is the time when the sun first shines; for sentient beings of the highest, most complete faculties, the unsurpassed fundamental wheel of Dharma is turned.

This is called the "Direct Manifestation Teaching" (*zhixian jiao*). It causes those who follow the One Vehicle of the Shared Teaching to transform their shared practice into the distinct [teaching], as follows:
When the sun first rises, it first illuminates the high mountains; this is the *Avataṃsaka* and *Brahmajāla* assemblies.

Second, as the sun ascends and shines further, for the sake of the three classes of sentient beings—low, middle, and high—it turns the Dharma-wheel that arises from the root to manifest the branches, causing those three classes of people to transform the three into one.
Just as there are heights and depths on the earth and mountains, there is a sequence of priority and posteriority in its successive illumination. Since this is so...
Between the beginning and the end, there must necessarily be a middle. Therefore, within this single period, it is further divided into three:

first, at the time of the initial turning, for the sake of sentient beings of inferior faculties, he turned the wheel of the Hīnayāna, which is called the "teaching that conceals the reality," causing those ordinary people and non-Buddhists [to attain realization].
Transforming the ordinary into the holy is like the sun’s first turning upward, illuminating the Black Mountains; this is the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* assembly (*Ekottarika Āgama*).
During the second turning, for the sake of sentient beings of middling capacity, the wheel of the Three Vehicles is turned;

this is called the "Teaching of Attraction and Inclusion," which causes those of the Two Vehicles to transform the small into the great, just as the sun’s midday turning illuminates the high plateaus. This is the Vaipulya [Sūtras].

This is the Secret Assembly. During the third turning of the wheel, for the sake of sentient beings of superior capacity, the Mahāyāna wheel of Dharma is turned; this is called the Teaching of Interfusion.
It causes those of the three vehicles to transform their provisional [teachings] into the Real, just as when the sun rises and its subsequent turning shines universally upon the great earth.

This is precisely the Assembly of Wondrous Wisdom Prajñā. These three preceding periods are like the rising sun, which gradually turns and gradually illuminates; therefore, they are collectively treated as a single period.
When the sun sets on the third day and shines again, for the sake of sentient beings of the highest capacity, the Dharma-wheel that gathers the branches back to the root is turned;
this is called the Teaching of the Opening of the Assembly. It causes those people of the five vehicles who follow partial teachings to transform their partiality into perfection, just as...
When the sun sets, it again shines upon the high mountains; this refers to the assemblies of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Nirvāṇa*.

Taken collectively, these constitute ten [assemblies], but to avoid prolixity, they are not cited here. As for the present sutra, it should have been preached during a later period within the distinct [teachings].
Nevertheless, there are two grounds for this: first, regarding time; second, regarding the Dharma.
Regarding the approximate date: the *Caixin jing* (Sutra on the Causes and Conditions) states that the Buddha and King Prasenajit were born on the same day.
Since King Prasenajit now recounts his own age as sixty-two years, the World-Honored One must also be sixty-two years old.

This would correspond to the thirty-second year after his enlightenment. At this point, twelve years of the *Āgama* period have already passed, and eight years of the *Vaipulya* period have also elapsed.

[The *Prajñāpāramitā*] has passed. Twenty-two years have already elapsed, with half of that period having passed; thus, it is certain that the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* was preached later, during the latter half of the assembly of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
[Question: How should the matters concerning Sunakṣatra and Virūḍhaka be reconciled? [Answer: In the *Bao’en jīng* (Sūtra on Requiting Kindness), Upāli asks: "How does the Buddha preach all things?

Does he preach according to the occasion, meeting the needs of the time and acting as is appropriate, or does he preach according to specific categories and groups? The Buddha answers: "The Buddha preaches all dharmas by adapting to the capacities of beings and the requirements of the time. Later, the disciples compiled the Dharma-piṭaka..."

They were compiled according to their categories. In the present sutra, the accounts of Sunakṣatra and Vaidūrya are recorded at the conclusion of the sutra’s title; perhaps these were taught at different times, and the compilers collected them under this same category. Furthermore, it is asked: "The ancient masters judge this to consist of two assemblies.

Those prior to the conclusion of the sutra are said to have been taught during the period of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, while those following the conclusion of the sutra are said to have been taught during the period of the *Nirvāṇa*. What do you, Master, think of this? I answer: There is nothing incorrect in this. However, when the Tathāgata preached the Dharma, there was both the primary teaching and the supplementary teaching.

In the present sutra, based on what Ānanda requested, the Tathāgata only taught the three names beginning with *śamatha*. If one can indeed rely on these to give rise to faith, develop understanding, and initiate practice, then the ocean of wondrous adornment will naturally be realized.

Having entered [the teaching], the names of the questions and answers are thus concluded right here; it would seem there is nothing further to be said. As for the meticulous investigation of the seven destinies (*sapta-gati*), the detailed discernment of the five demons (*pañca-māra*), and the repeated naming of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), these are intended for those who are unable to give rise to faith, develop understanding, or initiate practice.

This was taught as a supplementary provision for precautionary measures; it is not the primary intent. Even if it were spoken at a different time, it need not be judged separately, because one follows the primary teaching rather than the supplementary.
Regarding the Dharma, according to what Ānanda requested, this is the method by which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attain Bodhi; therefore, it naturally does not belong to the Āgamas.
Because the Āgamas belong to the Hīnayāna teachings, and furthermore, Ānanda said: "The World-Honored One also once expounded this meaning on Mount Laṅkā for Mahāmati and others, saying:
'Those non-Buddhists always speak of spontaneity (svabhāva), but I speak of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), which is not within their realm.
Since he says "once," it is a retrospective account of past events; from antiquity, all have used the *Laṅkāvatāra* as the definitive authority.
Since it belongs to the Vaipulya class, it is clear that this sutra was not taught during the Vaipulya period.

Furthermore, after the Tathāgata had used the analogy of the house and sought its door for Ānanda, the sūtra’s compiler describes how he took pity on those in the assembly—the pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas—who were not yet masters of the bodhicitta.
However, since they are said to be "not yet masters of the bodhicitta," they would naturally have been incapable [of receiving such teachings].
Since they are granted the prediction of attaining Buddhahood, it is clear that this sutra does not belong to the period of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

It has not even reached the stage of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, let alone the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, which was preached after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Therefore, it naturally should not be connected [to them]. (Question: After the section on "Breaking" (the *Zhongbie*), Ānanda erroneously established a passage on "Non-attachment," stating:

"In the past, I saw the Buddha together with his four great disciples—Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, and Śāriputra—turning the wheel of Dharma. They constantly spoke of awakening to and discerning the nature of the mind, saying that it is neither within..."

"It is not in the outside; it is not in the middle. Yet the *Shu* (Commentary) states: "In the past, I saw the Buddha point to the time when he turned the teaching of the *Prajñā*. Since this refers to a former occasion, does it not follow that the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* does not belong to the *Prajñā* [period]?

Why then is it judged to be among the teachings of the later turning? Is there an explanation for this? Answer: The various sections of the *Prajñāpāramitā* span twenty-two years. Perhaps what Ānanda cited belongs to the first half of the *Prajñā* assembly. To refer to the earlier period in contrast to the later is also permissible to call it "the past.

Therefore, the former statement—that the *Śūraṅgama* was spoken during the later turning—refers to the latter half of the *Prajñā* assembly. This concludes the discussion on the chronological sequence of the teachings.
Eighth, regarding the translators and commentators: from the West to the East, those who transmitted these teachings were willing to risk their very lives;

those who translated the Sanskrit into Chinese were all those who had taken vows and received the Buddha’s entrustment. As for the commentaries and exegeses, there has never been a lack of individuals throughout the generations.
The founder’s task is difficult; for one who follows and practices it, the task is easy. One must not say that each subsequent wisdom is superior to the preceding;

rather, one must know that the merit of each preceding stage is twice that of each subsequent one. To drink water and remember its source, I have thus set forth this account. The details of the translations and the monastic histories shall be reserved for the following section.
Although the records and chronicles differ in their oral traditions, since the times are distant and the people long gone, it is enough that there be even a single point upon which to rely.
The more one attempts to discern it, the more confused it becomes. Since it is impossible to raise the ancients from the dead to question them, such an endeavor seems unnecessary.
